description: How market pull and technology push drive new products and change industry.
content_html:
What Drives New Technology?

Design and technology does not stand still. Every year, new materials, manufacturing methods and digital tools change the products we use and the way designers work. Understanding why new technologies emerge is as important as knowing what they are. Two key forces drive technological change: market pull and technology push.

Market Pull

Market pull happens when consumers want something that does not yet exist, or want an existing product to work better. The demand comes first; designers and engineers then create a solution. A clear example is the growth of electric vehicles. Public concern about air quality and fossil fuel costs created strong consumer demand for cleaner transport long before carmakers had perfected battery technology. Manufacturers responded by investing heavily in development because the market was pulling them towards the solution.

Market pull is closely linked to the product life cycle. When a product reaches maturity or decline, consumer demand for something better creates a new pull. Smartphone makers release updated handsets annually partly because consumers expect incremental improvements — better cameras, longer battery life, faster processors. This demand is the market pulling the next iteration into existence.

Key Fact

Market pull means consumer or societal demand drives the development of a new product. The market need exists before the product is created.

Technology Push

Technology push works in the opposite direction. Scientists or engineers make a discovery or develop a new capability, and this creates products that consumers did not know they needed. The touchscreen was developed through research into capacitive materials before the first smartphone existed. Once the technology was ready, designers built products around it — consumers then discovered they wanted it.

Dyson’s cyclonic vacuum technology is a well-known example of technology push. James Dyson developed the cyclonic separation principle — using centrifugal force to spin dust out of an airstream without a bag — and then built a product around it. Consumers had not asked for a bagless vacuum; the technology created the market opportunity.

Additive manufacturing — commonly called 3D printing — is a clear case of technology push. Fused deposition modelling (FDM) was developed in the late 1980s for industrial prototyping. Consumers had no concept of printing physical objects at home. As the technology matured and costs fell, desktop 3D printers became available to schools, small businesses and hobbyists. The technology pushed itself into new markets that had not previously existed. Today, 3D printing is used in aerospace (Airbus uses additive manufacturing for lightweight aircraft components), medicine and consumer goods. This shows how a technology push in one industry can ripple into many others.

Consumer Choice and the Global Market

Modern consumers can buy products from anywhere in the world, which affects how designers work. Global production means a single product might be designed in one country, manufactured using components from several others, and sold worldwide. This creates both opportunities and responsibilities. Lower production costs in some regions allow more people to access well-designed products. However, global supply chains also raise questions about workers’ rights, fair wages and environmental standards.

Consumer choice is also shaped by legislation — laws that set standards for safety, energy efficiency and environmental impact. Regulations such as minimum energy performance standards for appliances mean that designers must meet legal requirements, not just consumer preferences. Legislation can therefore act as an additional driver of technological change, pushing manufacturers to develop cleaner or safer products.

Key Fact

Legislation sets minimum standards that products must meet — for example, safety regulations, energy efficiency rules and restrictions on hazardous materials. This forces designers to innovate even when there is no direct consumer demand for change.

Moral, Ethical and Cultural Factors

Technology does not exist in a vacuum. New products raise moral and ethical questions that designers must consider. Planned obsolescence — designing products to have a limited lifespan so consumers buy replacements — generates profit but also waste. Many consumers now actively consider the environmental and ethical record of the brands they buy from, pushing companies to adopt more responsible practices.

Apple’s approach to industrial design under Jonathan Ive became a case study in using aesthetics and material quality to command premium pricing, shaping consumer expectations across the electronics industry. At the same time, Apple’s supply chain practices were scrutinised for working conditions in factories, highlighting the ethical dimension of global production.

A common exam error is writing vague statements such as “make the product more eco-friendly.” Examiners look for specific, actionable improvements — for example, “replace virgin polymer components with recycled HDPE to reduce resource extraction” or “design for disassembly so materials can be separated and recycled at end of life.” The more precise and technically grounded the suggestion, the higher the mark. This applies equally to questions about new technologies — always name a specific technology and explain how it achieves the benefit, not just that it “helps the environment.”

The Product Life Cycle and Enterprise

The product life cycle moves through introduction, growth, maturity and decline. New and emerging technologies extend product life cycles by enabling redesign and improvement. Modular electronics, for instance, let manufacturers update components rather than replace entire devices. This has implications for enterprise — businesses must constantly monitor where their products sit in the life cycle and invest in the next generation before current products reach decline.

Emerging technologies also create new enterprise opportunities. Crowdfunding platforms now allow small designers to test market pull before committing to full-scale manufacture. If a product concept attracts enough backers, the designer has evidence of demand before spending on tooling or materials. This lowers the risk of bringing a new technology to market.
exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to ‘explain’ the impact of a new technology, always identify whether it is driven by market pull or technology push — then give a named example and explain the consequence for industry or consumers. For extended writing, avoid phrases like “it helps the environment” and instead specify the action: “replacing fossil-fuel-derived nylon with recycled polyester reduces landfill waste and carbon emissions.” Examiners award marks for precision, not for broad claims.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Market pull means consumer demand drives new product development; technology push means a scientific advance creates new product opportunities. Both forces shape the products we use every day.
  • Global production lowers costs but raises ethical questions about workers’ rights and environmental standards — legislation sets minimum standards designers must meet.
  • The product life cycle (introduction → growth → maturity → decline) helps businesses decide when to invest in new technology. Vague sustainability claims in the exam earn no marks — always name a specific action.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes 'technology push'?
A) Consumers demand a product that does not yet exist
B) Legislation forces manufacturers to change their products
C) A new scientific discovery creates products consumers had not asked for
D) A product reaches the decline stage of its life cycle
practice_questions.marks: C) A new scientific discovery creates products consumers had not asked for [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the four stages of the product life cycle.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for any two correct stages; two marks for all four:
• Introduction
• Growth
• Maturity
• Decline
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how global production can affect the design of a consumer product.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks for developed points including:
• Components can be sourced from multiple countries, allowing designers to select the most cost-effective or highest-quality supplier (1 mark). This reduces production cost but can make quality control more complex (1 mark additional development).
• Designers must consider varying safety and environmental legislation in different export markets (1 mark).
• Cultural differences between markets may require design modifications to meet local preferences or requirements (1 mark).
[Max 3 marks; each developed point = 1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain how consumer choice has influenced the development of electric vehicles. Refer to the concept of market pull in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
For each developed point award 2 marks (1 for basic point + 1 for development):
• Consumer concern about air quality and rising fuel costs created demand for cleaner transport before the technology was fully developed (1). Manufacturers invested in battery research because the market was pulling them towards a solution (1).
• Environmental legislation (e.g. emissions standards in cities) reinforced consumer demand by making petrol and diesel vehicles less attractive (1), accelerating investment in EV infrastructure and design (1).
[4 marks total; 2 marks per developed point]

practice_questions.text: Compare the advantages and disadvantages of designing products for a global market rather than a local one.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced discussion of advantages (economies of scale, wider consumer base, access to lower-cost components) and disadvantages (complex supply chains, ethical concerns over working conditions, need to meet multiple national standards). Reach a supported judgement about which factors matter most.
Secure: At least two developed advantages and two developed disadvantages with some specific context (e.g. a named material or sector).
Developing: Points made but limited development; mostly one side or both sides listed without balance.
Emerging: Simple statements with minimal explanation; no judgement reached.
[8 marks — levels-based]

practice_questions.text:
A sportswear manufacturer is considering using a new smart fabric that changes colour when the wearer overheats. The fabric has been developed by a research laboratory and is not yet widely available.

Evaluate whether introducing this new technology to the mass market is a realistic commercial decision for the manufacturer. Consider the product life cycle, market pull/technology push, consumer rights and legislation in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Thorough evaluation linking technology push (lab development before demand), product life cycle (introduction phase risks), relevant legislation (safety/labelling requirements), and consumer willingness to pay. Reaches a justified, balanced conclusion with specific technical and commercial reasoning.
Secure: Addresses at least three of the four areas with development; clear conclusion though it may not be fully nuanced.
Developing: Two areas addressed with some development; conclusion present but unsupported.
Emerging: One or two simple points; no real evaluation or conclusion.
[10 marks — levels-based]

knowledge_checks.q: What is 'market pull' in product development?
options: A scientific discovery that creates new product opportunities
Consumer or societal demand that drives the creation of a new product
A government regulation forcing product redesign
A drop in manufacturing cost that enables mass production

knowledge_checks.q: Which example best illustrates technology push?
options: Consumers demand longer-lasting smartphone batteries, so manufacturers develop improved cells
Cyclonic separation technology is invented and then used to create the first bagless vacuum
A safety regulation requires all toys to meet a flammability standard
Falling plastic costs allow manufacturers to make cheaper packaging

knowledge_checks.q: When a product reaches the decline stage of its _____, consumer demand for something better can create a new market pull.
Legislation sets _____ standards that products must meet, such as energy efficiency rules, even when consumers have not demanded change.
Match each term to its correct description:
right: Consumer or societal demand drives new product development
A scientific advance creates products consumers had not requested
The stages a product passes through from launch to decline

flashcard_questions.a: When consumer or societal demand drives the development of a new product.
When a scientific discovery creates new product opportunities consumers had not asked for.

flashcard_questions.q: Dyson's bagless vacuum is an example of market pull or technology push?
flashcard_questions.a: Technology push — cyclonic separation was invented before consumers requested a bagless cleaner.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the four stages of the product life cycle?
Which stage of the product life cycle is characterised by falling sales?
How did consumer concern about air quality drive EV development?
flashcard_questions.a: It created market pull — demand for cleaner transport pushed manufacturers to invest in battery technology.

flashcard_questions.q: Why must designers consider legislation when selling products globally?
flashcard_questions.a: Different countries have different safety, energy efficiency and environmental standards products must meet.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Airbus use additive manufacturing (3D printing) for in aircraft production?
flashcard_questions.a: To produce lightweight components, reducing aircraft weight and fuel consumption.
Designing products with a limited lifespan so consumers buy replacements more frequently.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do examiners reject 'make it more eco-friendly' as a sustainability suggestion?
flashcard_questions.a: It is too vague — a specific action (e.g. use recycled HDPE) is required to earn credit.

flashcard_questions.q: How can crowdfunding help a designer test market pull before manufacture?
flashcard_questions.a: Backers pledge money before production, proving demand exists before tooling costs are committed.

flashcard_questions.q: Apple's industrial design under Jonathan Ive is cited in the spec for which reason?
flashcard_questions.a: His approach used aesthetics and material quality to shape consumer expectations across the electronics industry.

glossary_terms.definition: When demand from consumers or society creates the need for a new or improved product.
When a new scientific discovery or invention creates opportunities for products that did not previously exist.
The stages a product goes through from its introduction to the market, through growth and maturity, to eventual decline.
